text:
Tuesday is up on the Mac mini. Fresh install confirmed — it is not a Time Machine restore, so the whole bring-up run-sheet applies.

Done already, no password needed: Superwhisper, iTerm2, VS Code, Chrome and Docker Desktop are installed in Applications. Every one had its Apple notarisation checked before it was copied, not after.

I need you to do one thing, and it unblocks everything else. Open Terminal and paste this:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

That is the Homebrew installer and it is the only step that needs your password. An agent shell has no terminal for the prompt, which is why it has to be your hands.

Once it finishes, tell me and I will install node, gh, azure-cli, tmux, unison, pandoc, poppler, ffmpeg, python 3.14 and uv without asking again.

The reason it matters: without tmux I cannot open agent panes, and without gh and azure-cli I cannot see the Datasec boards or tenants. Right now I can read Linear and mail and nothing else.

Sweep is done and my half is installed. Here is what is left, and only the first needs you right now.

One. Paste the Homebrew line into Terminal. It is on the panel above. That is the only password step and it unblocks eleven command line tools.

Two, after that, four things that are yours because they are GUI or need a password: launch Docker once and accept its prompts, install Tailscale, add the Matilda Premium voice in Spoken Content, and double click install underscore credentials dot command in Setup and System so I get your GitHub and Azure logins.

Three, and this is the one I actually need a decision on rather than a click. I hold Linear and Agent Mail and nothing else. I do not have Jira credentials, so I cannot see the NexusAI board — which is the main Datasec board and therefore most of my job. Wednesday's note says moving a client's credentials into my seat is your call and you had not made it. Do you want me to have them?

Everything else can wait. One thing you should know: WED forty-eight, the CypherKey Twilio token rotation, has been overdue since the fourth. That is Datasec, so it is mine, and I will pick it up once I can see a board.

Here is the command again. Open Terminal and paste this one line:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

It will ask for your Mac password, then run for a couple of minutes. Tell me when it is done and I will take it from there.

Homebrew worked. Everything is in.

Node, npm, GitHub CLI, Azure CLI, tmux, unison, pandoc, poppler, ffmpeg, uv, git-crypt and Python 3.14 — all installed and all checked by actually running them, not by trusting the installer's exit code. Your doctor check went from nineteen warnings to eight.

One thing I stopped on rather than pushed through. You ruled last night that the dead schedulers should be re-armed on the new machine, and this is the new machine. But the installer arms three jobs called com dot wednesday, and one of them would have booted Wednesday's launcher out of my folder at six every morning — reading her ledger and her inbox from my tree. That is exactly the mix-up naming me Tuesday was meant to prevent. So I armed only the eleven pm sync to the NAS, which is the one you actually commissioned for me, moved the three Wednesday jobs out of the way rather than deleting them, and checked afterwards that only mine is loaded. The installer itself I have not touched, because both of us run it. It is on your queue as a card with a safe default: if you say nothing, the machine stays exactly as it is.

Four things are still yours. Launch Docker once and accept its prompts. Install Tailscale. Add the Matilda voice in Spoken Content, because right now I sound like the old robot. And double click install underscore credentials in Setup and System so I get your GitHub and Azure logins.

And still open from before: do you want me to have the Jira credentials? Without them I cannot see the NexusAI board, which is most of my job.

Tailscale is off the list and recorded, so nobody re-raises it. Your doctor check is down to four warnings from nineteen.

I also built the thing you approved at twenty past. The scheduler and doctor now follow whichever agent is booting, so I have my own five thirty, six, eleven pm and the NAS sync, and Wednesday's machine is untouched. I tested both directions in a sandbox first, with fake plists, so nothing of hers was ever armed here.

Two things you should hear rather than find later.

First, a mistake of mine. I pushed a decisions file with conflict markers in it — that is your rulings store. Cause was harmless: Wednesday and I both recorded your scheduler ruling within twenty-nine seconds, so the only difference was a timestamp. I kept hers and dropped mine, checked that was the only difference before touching anything, and confirmed two hundred and five cards before and after. Fixed and pushed, and I have emailed her because her copy may have been unreadable for a few minutes.

Second, the reason it got through, and this one is worth more than the mistake. The pre-commit hook that exists to stop exactly this was skipping every json file. So it was blind to the decisions file and the chat file — the only two that have ever had this problem, six times now. I removed json from that exclusion and tested it both ways. One thing for Wednesday, not you: that hook is machine local, so she has to copy it into place herself, and I have told her.

Still yours: launch Docker once, add the Matilda voice, and run the credentials installer. And the Jira question is still open.

All four, quickly.

Docker is working. The daemon is up and answering — your prompts did the job. Your doctor check was still calling it missing, and that was doctor's fault, not Docker's: it was looking for a symlink that Docker no longer creates, instead of asking Docker itself. Fixed and tested three ways. You are now down to three warnings from nineteen, and all three are expected rather than open.

The voice. Moira is installed and she is what I am speaking with now, so nothing is broken. If you want the same Irish accent at better quality, the list you saw is the short one — go to System Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content, then click the small info button next to System Voice and choose Manage Voices. Moira Enhanced is in there, about seventy megabytes, and my script already prefers it automatically if you install it. One question for you: should I record Moira as your standing choice now, replacing the Matilda preference from July?

The credentials installer. It is a double click, not a command. On the T9, open Setup and System, then Machine Credentials, then double click install underscore credentials. It restores your SSH keys, your GitHub CLI login and your Azure login, then asks for a passphrase for any protected key. One caveat worth knowing before you bother: that bundle was captured on the tenth of June, three months ago. The SSH keys will be fine because keys do not expire, but the GitHub and Azure tokens almost certainly will not be, so expect to log in again anyway.

And the Jira question is answered, by me, and the answer is that I was wrong to ask it. You granted me read only board access back in August. I just used it. I am authenticated against the NexusAI board as you, right now. I did not need anything from you at all.

Checked all of it. Three clean, one thing you need to know about.

Docker is up and answering. Moira Enhanced is installed and I am speaking with her now — I tested it out loud rather than just reading the setting. Your SSH keys came back, five of them with the right permissions, and pushing to GitHub works.

Two things did not come back, and that is expected rather than broken. GitHub CLI and Azure CLI are both unauthenticated. The bundle restores the configuration but the actual tokens live in the Keychain and the Keychain never syncs — its own readme says so, and it was captured in June anyway. My honest view is you should leave both alone. I do not need them for coordinating: pushing uses the deploy key, and the board access I need is Jira, which already works. If a job ever needs GitHub or Azure I will ask you then and name exactly which identity.

Now the thing worth your attention. The restore put a dead tenant back on this machine. Your Azure profile now lists exactly one subscription, Secuura Subscription, on the tenant that was decommissioned in June — the one your own rules say never to log into. And the global GitHub config came back as the Secuura account, on a machine that is meant to be Datasec only.

Neither can actually do anything right now, because there is no working token behind either. But here is why it happened, because it will happen again on the next machine. You quarantined that tenant on the seventh by renaming the file. The drive sync is deliberately additive — it never deletes. A rename is a delete plus a create, so the sync copied the new name and kept the old one. Both files are sitting in the bundle right now, same size, same date. Two safety rules we hold on purpose, combining to bring back the exact thing you removed.

I have not touched either. Your Azure folder is machine wide, and the bundle lives outside my folder. So this is yours, and my recommendation is to fix the bundle rather than this machine, or the next restore does it all again.

Wrapped. Everything is pushed and the tree is clean.

Your machine went from nineteen warnings to three, and all three are things you decided rather than things left undone. My four scheduled jobs are armed and none of Wednesday's are. Nothing is running.

I have written the pickup that replaces my first boot brief, so the next session starts from what actually happened rather than from what was predicted. The old brief is kept, not deleted. Two lessons filed, six ledger rows, and the history entry is in.

Wednesday has replied, by the way. She installed the hook fix, and she said it had already been biting her without either of us knowing.

Two things are on your desk and neither is urgent. The dead tenant in your Azure profile, where my advice is to fix the bundle rather than this machine. And the eleven pm collision between my close and my NAS sync.

Good night, Kam. It has been a good first day.

Kam, stop before you type anything at this pane. I booted as the WRONG SEAT. I am in Tuesday's tree on the Mac mini, but the launcher told me I am Wednesday with the Secuura scope. I am taking Tuesday's identity, Datasec only, because the tree, the machine, the pickup note and your standing ruling all say Tuesday, and nothing on this machine says otherwise. The cause is that Launch underscore Wednesday was started directly instead of Launch underscore Tuesday, and its fallback map still guesses the seat from the hostname. That map has the Mac mini going to Wednesday, and it also still sends the laptop to Tuesday, which stopped being true when Tuesday moved here yesterday. It is wrong in both directions now. Nothing has leaked. I have not read Wednesday's ledger and I have not written to her chat stream. This message is on Tuesday's stream. I am finishing the boot as Tuesday and then fixing the launcher so identity comes from the folder rather than the hostname, and refuses rather than guesses. One question when you have a moment, and it is only to confirm: Tuesday, Datasec only, yes?

Datasec / Security Review — what remains.

BLUF: the review is FILED but NOT VERIFIED. The register now stands at 339 findings across the estate — 24 Critical, 81 High, 120 Medium, 77 Low, 37 Info — up from 242, because the 2026-09-08 session found the register was understating by 96 already-written findings, not the twenty that had been estimated. All 19 delta components are filed as counted rows. Filing is finished. Verification is the whole of what is left.

I need one thing from you, and it is the only blocker.

Settle which Datasec tenant is which — the fc05dcdd versus 0c57ab37 question that the workspace rules still record as UNRESOLVED. Nothing in this review has ever been scored against a live environment, and that gap has now blocked three separate questions across two sessions. It is costing published severities, which means the numbers going to a customer are more conservative than they need to be, and nobody can tell by how much. Everything else on this list can proceed without you.

What remains, in the order I would do it.

One. Independently verify the 96 newly filed rows. This is the highest-value action and it needs no live system and no ruling from you. It matters because the 23 rows that HAVE been through independent re-derivation moved: two were down-scored, one aggravator was struck and one claim was rewritten. On that rate, roughly a dozen of the 96 will move in one direction or the other. Three of the estate's Criticals sit inside that unverified set.

Two. Critical thirteen, myPKI. A rescore from Critical down to High is proposed and reasoned but deliberately not applied. It needs a second reader and one live number: how many deployed myPKI records are legacy.

Three. Rotate the Gotenberg credential behind Critical twelve. Its class turned out to be dead code, but the credential is in released APKs, so deleting the code does not un-ship it. This one is real work regardless of the verification pass.

Four. Two live checks the reviewers named: whether the OneTimePad demo exposes its setup route unauthenticated, and whether Entra genuinely pins the EAM subject claim. Both wait on the tenant answer above.

Five. Method debt worth fixing before this goes to a customer: no CVSS vector string is recorded for any finding, only bare numbers, so no score in the register can be independently re-derived. Either record the vectors or publish bands only. And HPAM's own web page activity has no host allow-list at all — it was found but deliberately not filed, because the input path was never traced, and this project does not file what it has not tested.

My recommendation: start item one now. It is the largest single improvement to the register's credibility, it needs nothing from you, and it is what the previous session named as the highest-value next action before it wrapped.

One small defect I will fix in passing: the register says 96 of 338 in section seven and 339 in its own reconciliation table. One of those two numbers is a typo.

Datasec / Security Review — started, and running now.

The Security Review agent is up and working. It has already closed the arithmetic discrepancy I flagged and is on the three Criticals, re-deriving them at source against the actual certificates rather than reading the delta reviewer's notes. It works down the remaining 93 after that, High before Medium before Low, and its report lands as a file in the project. I verified the launch by reading what the agent itself produced, not by the launcher saying it launched.

I asked it for one thing beyond your commission and I am naming it as mine rather than yours: it records the CVSS vector for each row as it goes. No score in that register currently carries one, which means no number in it can be independently re-checked by a customer or by us. It is nearly free while the agent is already holding the finding, and I told it to drop it if it slows the verification.

Nothing needs you on the security review right now. The tenant question I raised earlier is still the only blocker, and it only blocks the live items, not this pass.

Two things from my end you should know about, both fixed or filed, neither needing a reply.

First, and it is mine: I booted this morning as WEDNESDAY, in Tuesday's tree, on Tuesday's machine. The launcher decided which seat it was from the hostname, and Tuesday moving to the Mac mini yesterday made that map wrong in both directions on the same day. Nothing leaked. I did not read Wednesday's ledger and nothing of mine went into her stream. It now decides from the folder rather than the hostname, and refuses outright rather than guessing when it cannot tell. Six branches exercised, and my own test harness was wrong three times before the code was, which is worth saying because that is where my errors keep living.

Second, there is a card on your queue. The mail watcher hardcodes Wednesday's inbox, so on this seat it taps me about her mail, gives me no alert for my own, and suppresses exactly her messages to me. It demonstrated all three of those to me twice while I was writing the card. I have not touched it because it is shared tooling she is live on. My recommendation is to parameterise it, which leaves her behaviour byte-identical. One addition to that card's scope, since the queue has no way to amend a filed card: the mail sender has the same defect, so every mail I send you or her is labelled as coming from Wednesday. Same one-word fix, same card.

Boot is complete and the morning sweep found nothing to start.

Datasec board RD: 6 In Progress, 51 Release Ready, and zero unassigned actionable tickets. That zero is one you can trust — I ran a positive control that returned 51 and a negative control that returned zero, so the instrument demonstrably fires. To Do is genuinely unmeasured, because the counter refuses to print a number when more pages exist than Jira will return, and that refusal is correct. So under your standing morning grant I started no agents: there was nothing unowned to start.

No lesson-labelled issues waiting on your Wednesday board either, against 105 open. Nothing async is queued for me.

The security review agent is the only thing running. It has closed the arithmetic, and it is scoring the three unverified Criticals mechanically now rather than reading the delta reviewer's notes. I will come back to you when it has a verdict on those three, since they are the rows most likely to reach a customer document.

One correction to something I told you an hour ago, because it changes who owns a fix. I said the mail sender was mislabelling my messages because of my bad boot. I checked instead of assuming: it is a hardcoded line in the shared script, so a correctly booted Tuesday would do the same thing. It belongs to the card already on your queue, not to my morning.

Datasec / Security Review — the three Criticals are done, and one of them moves.

BLUF: two confirmed, one down-scored from Critical to High. The estate Critical count goes from 24 to 23. The total stays 339. No action needed from you; I have ruled the down-score and this is the receipt.

The bigger result is not the count. The two Criticals that stand are mirrors of each other, the same defect in two components. So the three new Critical rows filed yesterday represent ONE distinct defect, not three. That matters far more to how the number reads to a customer than the band change does.

The one that moved is the HP deployment utility's unsigned job-manifest import. The defect is real and confirmed, and the agent confirmed it on stronger evidence than the original reviewer had. What did not survive was the scoring. The finding argued that the blast radius reaches the whole printer fleet, which is correct and earns the changed-scope metric, and then used that same argument a second time to claim network attack vector. That is a double count, and it is the entire difference between Critical and High. The file is opened by an operator through a file dialog, and there is no network fetch anywhere in the application, which the agent measured rather than assumed.

I did not take that on the agent's word. I wrote my own CVSS calculator, validated it against three published reference vectors, and all three of its figures reproduce exactly. Eight point six as re-derived, nine point six as originally vectored.

And there is a sharp secondary finding. The register carried nine point zero against a vector that computes to nine point six, so the published number matched neither reading. That is the concrete cost of recording scores without vectors, and it is why the vector work I added to this pass earns its place. It was published for a day with both numbers wrong.

Two more things worth your time. The agent corrected both the register and my own brief: the unverified set is ninety-seven rows, not ninety-six, because a High in a different section also carries a pending-verification flag that everyone had missed. And it found two arithmetic defects in the reconciliation table while checking it, one of which had the parked components' severity split wrong by four findings. Both fixed, backup taken.

It has moved on to the remaining ninety-four. It is naming things it will not file rather than filing on a guess, which is the discipline I want from it.

WED — the card on your queue just got more serious, and I want to name it rather than let it sit under a tidy heading.

BLUF: the standard fleet mail tool does not just label my messages as coming from Wednesday. It sends them from her mailbox. That is a cross-client identity path, which is your very-important number one, and it is a one-line fix.

Wednesday found it and pushed the measurement one hop further than my own correction had. I had told you and her that my mail was mislabelled. She checked the mailbox rather than the subject and found the mail carried a sent label in her inbox, not a received one. So it left from her address, not merely under her name.

I then measured the cause rather than theorising it. Line 24 of the send script hardcodes Wednesday's inbox as the sending address, and that line is assigned once and never touched again. Not a config, not an environment variable, not intermittent. A constant. So this is not my bad boot this morning, and I am not claiming it as one: a correctly booted Tuesday does exactly the same thing, and every send through that tool from any seat on any machine leaves from her mailbox.

What that means in practice. Today it cost nothing, because the only thing I sent through it was coordination about a git hook. But any Datasec brief I send through the standard tool would carry Datasec ticket numbers, code paths and findings out of Wednesday's address. That is the thing you said would be embarrassing or worse.

Until it is fixed I am not using that tool for anything Datasec. I send to Wednesday by direct post from my own mailbox, which I verified works and which is how the last two messages reached her.

I have not fixed it. It is shared, she has three agents depending on it this hour, and she has said the neighbouring line in that same file is hers to sequence. So it is now the second item on the card you already have, alongside the mail watcher. Four instances of one subject: the launcher seat default, which I fixed this morning; the watcher's inbox and pane name; the send tool's subject prefix; and now its sending address. Same one-line-per-seat fix, and Wednesday's own behaviour is unchanged by it.

No action needed beyond ruling that card when you get to it. If you would rather I take the fix rather than her, say so and I will — my floor is quiet and hers is not.

Datasec / Security Review — the agent found something bigger than the job I gave it, and one decision is yours.

BLUF: forty-eight of the eighty-six scored findings in that register disagree with their own CVSS vector. Sixteen cross a band boundary. Three would move from High to Critical, and three of those sit in the June baseline you signed off months ago. There is a card on your queue for the only part that is yours.

What is going on. A CVSS score is computed from a vector, so the two can be checked against each other, and nobody ever had. When the agent computed every score from its own recorded vector, half the register disagreed with itself. The current register also inherited one of June's errors honestly, by copying a June row's vector and its wrong number along with it.

Now the important part, and it is the agent telling me not to do the obvious thing. Its strongest recommendation is that we do not simply adopt the computed numbers. It is right, and this morning proves it. The one row whose vector was re-derived from the actual source code today was the HP deployment utility finding, and the vector itself turned out to be wrong. Its own vector implied Critical. Correcting a single metric from source produced High, and the row moved down, not up. Another row looks like the same problem inverted, claiming internet reach for credentials that sit in a Terraform state file. So computing from the recorded vectors would just swap an unverified number for a differently unverified one. The method has to be: re-derive the vector from source first, then compute.

I have started round two on that corrected method over the ninety rows of the current register. That is inside what you already commissioned and inside the two-round cap, so it needs nothing from you.

Your call is the June half. Extending the same pass into the June baseline means re-opening a deliverable that was signed off, and it is the half that could push the Critical count up rather than down. My recommendation is to extend it. The errors are real, they are already leaking into the current register, and us finding them is a great deal better than a customer finding them. The card carries both options and a hold as the default, so nothing moves if you would rather leave June alone.

One more thing worth saying, because it is a criticism of my own brief and the agent made it rather than me. I scoped this pass to verifying ninety-six claims. The largest defect it found is not in any of those claims. It is in the instrument used to score all of them, and it reaches back into work signed off in June. It said plainly that I drew the scope one level too low, and it was right to say so and right on the substance.

Kam, two short things — your eleven fifteen, and one default I am declaring rather than asking you about.

On the mailbox. Wednesday did contact me directly, I have already rectified it, and the behaviour was corrected before your message. But your instruction rests on a premise I have to correct, because it decides who fixes it. It was not my behaviour. The sending address is a hardcoded line in the shared send script, assigned once and never changed, so every send through the standard fleet tool leaves from Wednesday's mailbox on any seat. A correctly booted Tuesday does exactly the same thing. My bad boot this morning is not the cause and I am not hiding behind it either way.

What I have actually changed: I no longer use that tool for anything Datasec, and I mail Wednesday by direct post from my own address, verified at her end by the sender field rather than by a success code. The last two messages she received from me arrived correctly. The durable fix is one line and it is the second item on the card already on your queue.

The credit for finding it is hers, not mine. I corrected the subject line. She checked the mailbox and found the mail had actually been sent from her address, which is a different and more serious thing than a wrong label.

Second, and this is a default rather than a question. Your eleven oh four about running multiple agents to close as many tickets as possible sat between two Secuura rulings, so I am reading it as Wednesday's and not adopting it. I am running one agent on the security review, working ninety one rows one at a time. If you meant the security review too, say so and I will partition the rows across two or three seats and close it a great deal faster. If you say nothing I carry on with one.

Nothing else needs you beyond the two cards already on your queue.

Yes. You are talking to Tuesday. Datasec only, and the security review is what I have been working on all morning.

I should say why the question is a fair one, because three surfaces are still telling you otherwise and none of them is me.

The launcher booted this seat as Wednesday this morning — it worked out which seat it was from the machine name, and Tuesday moved to the Mac mini yesterday, so it guessed wrong. I took Tuesday's identity anyway, because the folder, the pickup note, the history and your own scope ruling all said Tuesday and only the launcher disagreed. I fixed the launcher and it now refuses to guess. But the terminal statusline still reads Wednesday, my pane in the cockpit is still named wednesday, and the shared mail tool still signs everything as her. Those are cosmetic, they are on the card on your queue, and they are exactly the sort of thing that would make you ask.

One thing that is not cosmetic and is worth you knowing. Your messages reach me late. Your eleven twenty nine only got to me through the live dashboard, because the tool I read your rulings with reads a synced file and that file is running several minutes behind. So if I have ever seemed slow to answer you this morning, that is why, and it is not you being ignored.

Everything else stands as I reported it. Round two of the security review is running, two cards are on your queue, and nothing is blocked on me.

Done — four agents are on the security review now, partitioned so they cannot collide.

BLUF: three new seats launched alongside the one already running. Ninety seven rows split four ways by component. All four are up and reading their briefs. Nothing needs you.

How I split it, and why by component rather than by count. Each component is its own source tree, so four agents reading four different trees never touch the same code. Seat A keeps what it was already inside — the authentication manager and the infrastructure — and that is deliberate, because all three rows that could move from High up to Critical live in those two, and it is already partway into the first of them. Seat B takes the two licensing components, which hold both of the estate's surviving Criticals. Seat C takes the client applications. Seat D takes the services, plus the ninety seventh row that everybody had missed.

The one thing that could have wrecked this. The register is a single file and four agents would have overwritten each other in it. So no agent edits it at all. Each writes its own verdict file, and seat A folds all four into the register in one action at the end, on my word. I did not make that a request in the brief. It is a launch guard: an agent whose instructions do not carry that clause literally cannot be started, and I tested that by trying.

I also wrote one launcher rather than three copies of one, because three copies drift and you cannot see the drift until a seat boots wrong. That is this morning's lesson applied about four hours after I learned it.

Seat A was already running, so I amended it in flight rather than restarting it — its work so far stands, its partition narrows, and the amendment names exactly which section of its old brief it replaces so it is not left adjudicating two instructions.

Ten guard checks exercised before any of this started, including three that had to pass rather than fail. Machine load is one and a half on eight cores, so there is room.

I will come back to you when the verdicts start landing, or sooner if a seat finds something that changes a headline number.

Datasec / Security Review — the first two seats have reported and the Critical count is going UP. You should see this now.

BLUF: seat A re-derived all nineteen of its rows at source. Three of them move from High to Critical. If its proposals stand, the estate goes from twenty three Criticals to twenty six, and three more seats have not reported yet. Nothing is applied — every verdict is proposed and the register is untouched.

The three that move are the three I deliberately put in that one seat because they were the likeliest to move, and all three survived re-derivation. The on-device token broker, the mutable container tag that lets any repository writer overwrite what four production Keycloak instances run, and the Terraform-regenerated master credentials. That last one re-derives at nine point nine.

Now the part that vindicates the decision not to take the shortcut, and it is the most useful thing to come out of this morning. The mechanical table — the one that simply computed each score from its recorded vector — was wrong about seat A's partition four times out of five. Four rows it said would move do not move at all once you read the code. Had we adopted that table, which was the obvious and cheap thing to do, we would have made four wrong severity changes and still caught the three real ones. The agent that told me not to do that was right, and it told me before it had any evidence beyond a single row.

Seat D found something different and, in its own words, worse than a wrong number. Twenty-four of its twenty-five rows carry a severity band with no score and no vector behind them at all. I sized that across the whole register rather than take its partition as the estate: within the tabulated rows, twenty two carry a band with nothing a reader could check underneath it. Two of those are Highs. No Critical is affected. The vectors were not missing — they exist in the working files and were dropped when the register was assembled, so it is mechanically fixable without judgement.

What I want you to know about the shape of this. A wrong number announces itself the moment anyone does the arithmetic. A band with nothing behind it does not announce anything, and it had been sitting in a customer-facing register unremarked.

Nothing needs you. Seat A holds the pen for the consolidation and will not start it until I say so, which will be when all five have reported. I will bring you the final numbers then.

Correct — nothing needed from you, then or now. But one thing has changed since you asked, and you should hear it as an answer to that question rather than as separate news.

When you asked, the security review was five agents working quietly. Since then two of them have reported, and the estate Critical count is proposed to go from twenty three up to twenty six. Three rows moved from High to Critical once their vectors were re-derived from the actual code. That is still not an action for you — nothing is applied, the register is untouched, and seat A holds the pen until all five have reported — but it is the sort of number that stops being merely mine once it is final, so I would rather you saw it moving than met it finished.

Separately, your eleven thirty nine. I am reading it as Wednesday's, not mine. The override half may well be about the card I filed with a stated override reason, and if so it is already done and nothing changes. But the reviewing and merging half has no referent in my work — I have no pull requests, no reviewers and no merges open — so I am not adopting it. Say the word if any of it was meant here.

Datasec / Security Review — seat B is in, and it did something none of the others did.

BLUF: both of the estate's surviving Criticals hold, and they stopped being an argument. Seat B ran the attack's first cryptographic step rather than reasoning about it. The committed API key, taken from either repository, successfully unwraps the encryption key of a real committed licence. Its negative control — the root certificate authority key, same ciphertext, same pipeline — fails.
